newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Sugar - China imports queried, region quiet.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China imports queried, region quiet.

text.p: Recent reported purchases of Thai raw sugar by China are not likely to be delivered because licences have not been granted to Chinese buyers and low prices make tolling unviable, traders said on Wednesday.
"People got excited, but China is not importing sugar," a trader with a big U.S. house in Hong Kong said.
Since February, China has reportedly bought four cargoes of Thai sugar for tolling, or processing and re-exporting.
But industry sources now say China has yet to issue sugar import licences, and the purchases from Thailand have been overstated by two-thirds.
One licence for 25,000 tonnes had been issued to the remote and impoverished Himalayan region of Tibet, a banking source in Hong Kong said.
This could not be immediately confirmed, although trade and industry sources throughout the region said they doubted China would take delivery of the reported Thai purchases.
Sugar prices in the southern growing regions have yet to reach break-even levels, a source in Guangxi province, where most of China's cane sugar is produced, said.
Ex-factory prices in Guangxi were seen at 3,950-3,980 yuan ($476-469) per tonne, the head of a big joint venture operation there said by telephone.
"There is an upward trend and hope is on the horizon," he said. He added that he expected prices of processed white sugar to move to 4,000-4,100 yuan ($482-494) a tonne within the next 30 days.
Prices would stabilise at that level before market supply tightened and shortages kicked in around August, he said.

In other Asian developments, Japanese traders said news the Philippines had been granted an additional sugar quota of 27,411 tonnes by the United States for the 1996/97 crop year ending in August had little effect on the market.
The U.S. Sugar Regulatory Administration, which grants quotas, said the original U.S. allocation to the Philippines for the current crop year was 219,000 tonnes.
The United States imports sugar from some countries at a premium to world prices.
"Total quota by the U.S. is fixed, and I don't expect much impact in the world market," a Tokyo sugar trader said.
Japanese traders said news that Philippine sugar millers were holding 100,000 tonnes of unsold stock in their warehouses was also unlikely to dampen the market.

Thai raw sugar premiums for May/July delivery quoted at 0.25/0.40 cents per pound (bid/offer), against 0.30/0.40 cents a week earlier, over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on a free on board (FOB) basis.
July/September deliveries were quoted at 0.60/0.90 cents.
"Asia's physical sugar market remains quiet. We heard some traders are quoting premium for March delivery at 0.10 cent, but this is exceptional," another sugar trader said.
-- Eiichiro Tokumoto, Tokyo Commodities Desk (81-3) 3432-7391
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai Newsroom (86-21)6279-8544
